newsitem.title: UK: Coffee prices reignite, gold is steadier.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices reignite, gold is steadier.

text.p: Coffee prices turned higher again on Monday after an uncertain start, suggesting to some traders that a rally that has taken them up by almost one-third this year has further to go.
Gold steadied just above $340 an ounce after dropping by some $30 since the start of 1997.

The sharp rise in the price of coffee beans, on concerns about low stocks and uncertain supplies from Latin America, has already led some roasters to make increases in retail prices to consumers, notably in Germany and the Netherlands.
The pace on Monday was set by trading in Arabica type futures in New York after news that there may be a strike by state workers in Colombia, a key producer.

Futures on the New York Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange erased opening losses and jumped to fresh life-of-contract highs as speculators bought heavily. The spot March Arabica contract rose 5.95 cents per pound to a new high of 157.00 before profit-taking.
"Technically, the market is strong," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast. She added that the Colombia news was "another event that will have short-term psychological impact."

Concerns that a strike may interrupt the flow of coffee out of the second-largest producer fuelled supply worries at a time when inventories hover at low levels and Brazil, the biggest supplier, may have a lower-than-expected crop.

Colombian armed forces are on alert ahead of a threatened strike on Tuesday which promises to be the largest in 20 years. Talks between union chiefs and government ministers aimed at averting the indefinite stoppage by more than 800,000 state workers broke down on Sunday.

But while some coffee brokers said a strike by government workers may have little impact on the Colombian coffee trade, they noted that in a bull market any news was likely to be viewed as constructive.
"Everything that comes out is construed as friendly," one trader said.

Last month, a dockworkers' strike in the Colombian port of Buenaventura helped fuel the market's bull run, as coffee exports were blocked and slow getting to normal following the nine-day work stoppage.
London Robusta coffee futures for May ended $45 per tonne up on the day at $1,585 but below values above $1,600 seen last week.
Oil prices, after a long bull run, remained under pressure. Bellwether North Sea Brent crude futures traded in London around $20.80 per barrel late in the British afternoon.

Last Friday saw Brent below $21 for the first time since last August. It reached a six-year high at $25 in October because of delays to resumed supply from Iraq and low stocks of heating fuel. Supply worries have now eased.
Cocoa weakened on reports of generous deliveries from Ivory Coast.
Among industrial metals aluminium eased on fund selling after it failed to hold technical support at $1,600 per tonne.
Gold was little changed on Monday but palladium traded at its highest level since early May last year on fund buying in New York.
"The funds like the look of this sort of market," a dealer said as palladium traded around $135.55/$136.55 per ounce.
Fund buying came in on the back of consumer covering against delays to the start of Russian-Japanse talks on settling their 1997 supply contract.
"Palladium is generally forecast to go higher because of the Russian issue," another dealer said.,
Russia is the world's leading supplier providing over 66 percent of needs while Japan accounted for over 40 percent of demand in 1995.
Palladium is used in electronic components, autocatalysts to clean up car exhaust fumes, dentistry and a wide variety of chemical applications.
